audio_caption: The clip begins with a male speaker expressing gratitude for the interview. A female speaker responds with a friendly acknowledgement before stating her intent to ask about his experiences in Congress and the presidency and seek advice for Ford School students.

The clip opens with a calm and welcoming tone from a female speaker who says, "Delighted." She proceeds to commend a male speaker on his long career in public service, especially his time as Vice President. The male speaker begins his response by identifying three "important ingredients" for success in public service, including "total integrity," "hard work," and the ability to get "good people to work with you." His tone is measured and thoughtful.

The audio clip features two speakers, a woman and a man, engaged in a conversation. The woman speculates that certain skills have remained unchanged, and the man concurs, stating, "I'm sure they're identical." He elaborates on potential improvements in communication due to computers while affirming that "the fundamentals are still there." The tone throughout is conversational and thoughtful.

The audio clip begins with a female speaker who expresses someone being known for their moral compass, asking about times they had to make a decision with moral elements. The speaker has a measured tone, asking questions with clear articulation. The audio quality is clear, allowing for distinct understanding of each word.

The audio clip features a single male speaker discussing his decision to pardon President Nixon, characterizing it as "probably the most notorious." He explains the decision was made "solely on my own judgement" and in "the national interest." He mentions spending a significant portion of his time as president dealing with Nixon's tapes and papers, arguing this diverted attention from other important issues. To "clear the decks" he decided to pardon Nixon and "get the matter out of my hands." A female speaker briefly responds. The overall speaking tone is measured and reflective.

The audio features a male speaker responding to an unseen interviewer about his presidency. The speaker has a reflective and somewhat nostalgic tone, discussing economic problems like high interest rates and inflation, describing them as a "bad economic circumstance". He speaks of developing an economic plan with Alan Greenspan to counter "stagflation." He believes they turned the economy around within a year.

The clip features a conversation between two speakers, a man and a woman, about economy. The woman acknowledges it as a good accomplishment and the man expresses how he advises students to have "good parental background," noting that his mother and stepfather were an inspiration to him to have integrity. He believes having parents that inculcate that kind of integrity is the best source and that over time you have to look at the compass and make sure you are following it in the right direction.

A male speaker begins, introducing "direction" in a thoughtful tone. He is followed by a female speaker, who acknowledges the speaker's insights and notes the roles of students as policy analysts and public managers, inquiring about effective collaboration with elected public servants. The male speaker responds, stressing the importance of a harmonious relationship between elected officials and appointed individuals, emphasizing that they "should be a team." The speaker shares experiences from his time in Congress, mentioning efforts to build relationships with public servants in various departments. The speaker concludes, saying that if there is good rapport between "elective and others" then you have done a good job on behalf of the country.

The audio clip features a conversation between two speakers, one male and one female. The female speaker begins by asking a question, referencing the male speaker's entry into Congress in the late 1940s and asking what has changed in public life, particularly in the way politics is conducted and in the issues that are considered. The male speaker responds, beginning with "Let me put it this way, Becky."

The audio clip begins with a male speaker expressing disappointment with the current political climate. He compares it unfavorably to his experiences in Congress in 1949, noting the increased bitterness and unhealthy partisan relationships, which he blames on an unidentified source. A female speaker follows, agreeing that this political environment makes life more difficult for her students who work in agencies, as they often get caught in political crossfires. The male speaker acknowledges the unfortunate nature of this situation and hopes that this partisan transitional period will evolve and be eliminated.

The audio clip features a conversation where a person, who seems to be giving advice to students, asks a question on preparing for a changing career.  A male speaker responds, saying it's a hard question, then discusses looking at the facts at the time, giving an example where if he were in Congress today, he would try to develop a rapport with democratic counterparts, referring to his own experiences working with speakers McCormick and Tip O'Neill, emphasizing debating issues and renewing personal friendships after debates, which he indicates was important for getting things done. A second voice then says Yeah.

The audio clip begins with a female speaker discussing a "byproduct of partisanship," specifically, "a reduced respect for public servants." She states that students talk about going into government, and will they get the respect in that career that they would really like to have? She asks if there are suggestions or advice as to how they or others can do things to "re-." The speaker speaks in a measured, thoughtful tone.
